summary: Describes SCRAM, a family of SASL and GSS-API mechanisms that let clients prove they know a password without sending it in the clear. It aims to fix problems that kept earlier challenge-response mechanisms from being widely deployed. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: SCRAM lets a client prove it knows a password without sending the password itself. The server also sends proof of its own, and optional channel binding can tie the login to the protected connection.

subtitle: A challenge-response login that proves password knowledge and can authenticate both client and server.

tldr.problem: Sending a password in clear text, even inside a protected channel, has security concerns. Earlier challenge-response mechanisms on the standards track did not meet the stated needs for broad deployment.
tldr.mechanism: SCRAM uses a client proof based on a salted, repeatedly hashed password and a server signature. It supports mutual authentication and can bind the exchange to an external secure channel.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5802 defines SCRAM for SASL and GSS-API and requires implementations to support SCRAM-SHA-1. It is updated by RFC 7677 and RFC 9266.

today: RFC 5802 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2010. It has been updated by RFC 7677 and RFC 9266.

sections.title: The Purpose of SCRAM
sections.content:
The Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism (SCRAM) is a family of authentication mechanisms for the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL). It also works as a Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) mechanism through the GS2 bridge.

SCRAM is designed to address concerns with sending clear-text passwords over a channel protected by Transport Layer Security (TLS). It is intended to run under an external security layer such as TLS or SSH; SCRAM itself does not negotiate a security layer.

The RFC says stored authentication information is not sufficient by itself to impersonate a client, and that salt protects against pre-stored dictionary attacks. SCRAM supports mutual authentication, authorization identities in SASL, and server-authorized proxies under the conditions described in the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: SCRAM lets a client prove knowledge of a password without sending that password. It is designed to run inside a separate protected connection, such as TLS.

sections.title: How the Password Proof Works
sections.content:
The server keeps authentication information for each user: a salt, an iteration count, a StoredKey and a ServerKey. The client starts with the username and password. After the server sends the salt and iteration count, the client computes a salted password and derives keys and a proof from it.

The client proof is calculated from the client key and a signature over the authentication messages. The server uses its stored key to check that proof. A successful check shows that the client has access to the password. The server also sends a ServerSignature; the client computes the expected value and compares it with the server's value.

Usernames and passwords must be encoded in UTF-8. The password is normalized using the SASLprep profile; implementations must either support SASLprep or disallow non-ASCII codepoints in the string.
sections.plainLanguage: The client calculates a proof from the password, and the server checks it against stored information. The server returns its own proof so the client can check the server too.

sections.title: The Four-Part Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
SCRAM messages are text containing comma-separated, one-letter attribute-value pairs. In a full exchange, the client sends its username and a random nonce. The server replies with its own nonce added to the client's, plus the user's salt and iteration count.

The client then sends the combined nonce, channel-binding data and ClientProof. The server checks the nonce and proof, checks any supplied authorization identity, and sends a final message containing a ServerSignature or an error. The client must fail the exchange if the server signature does not match its own calculation.

The attribute names are case-sensitive and their order is fixed, apart from extension attributes in their allowed positions. For SCRAM-SHA-1, servers should announce an iteration count of at least 4096.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server exchange four messages: an opening identity, a server challenge, a client proof and a server result. Each side checks a value that depends on the password-derived information.

sections.title: Mechanism Names and Channel Binding
sections.content:
A SCRAM mechanism name begins with SCRAM-, includes the uppercase name of its hash function, and may end with -PLUS. The suffix indicates a mechanism that uses channel binding to connect the authentication exchange to an external secure channel. All SCRAM clients and servers must implement SCRAM-SHA-1.

Servers that support channel binding should advertise both the plain and PLUS versions of a mechanism. The client signals whether it does not support channel binding, believes the server does not support it, or requires a named binding type. If the client indicates that it supports channel binding but believes the server does not, and the server actually supports it, the server must fail authentication to prevent a downgrade.

The default channel-binding type is tls-unique. A server implementing any channel binding must implement that type; clients should implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: Channel binding connects the login proof to the secure channel carrying it. The PLUS mechanism name signals that the client and server can use this extra check.

sections.title: SCRAM as a GSS-API Mechanism
sections.content:
SCRAM also defines a GSS-API mechanism. It uses the same authentication messages, with differences in the initial context token: the GS2 header and channel-binding data are omitted, and the GSS-API initial token header is added to the client's first message.

The mechanism OID for SCRAM-SHA-1 is 1.3.6.1.5.5.14. Its security contexts always support mutual authentication and do not support credential delegation. The RFC defines GSS-API principal-name handling, per-message tokens and a pseudo-random function for GSS-API implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC also adapts SCRAM for GSS-API software. The authentication messages remain similar, but the initial token has a different wrapper.

sections.title: Security Limits and Risks
sections.content:
Without a strong external security layer that provides confidentiality, an observer can collect enough information to attempt an offline dictionary or brute-force attack. Salt makes a stolen authentication database more costly to attack by requiring a separate attempt for each password, but it does not prevent password guessing.

An attacker who steals authentication information and also observes an exchange or impersonates a server may be able to impersonate that user to servers using the same hash function, password, iteration count and salt. The RFC therefore says salts should be generated randomly. It also warns that a hostile server can send an extremely large iteration count to consume client resources.

SCRAM provides no security layer of its own and does not protect against downgrade attacks on channel-binding types. The RFC discusses protecting mechanism negotiation through channel binding or an external channel that authenticates a user-provided server name.
sections.plainLanguage: SCRAM does not make password guessing impossible, especially if the stored authentication data is stolen. A protected connection, random salts and careful handling of server challenges remain important.
